intent: Function: the head walks right past each mark and marks the next blank, so three marks become four.
content: The head steps along three marks and turns the first empty cell into a fourth because two rules decide every step (on a mark, move right; on an empty cell, write and stop), so 3 + 1 = 4 is computed by rule-following alone.
knows: Tally marks; following written instructions one at a time.

intent: Real thing: the rotors step before each press, so the same key lights a different lamp every time.
content: One key lights a different lamp at each press because the rotors step before the current runs key, three rotors, reflector and back, so the same A gives F, then E, then C, and never A itself, the flaw the codebreakers used. The reflector sends the current back by another path, so no letter ever lights itself (ch1-context-p9), the flaw the codebreakers used.
knows: A typewriter keyboard; a battery lighting a bulb through a wire.
subtraction: Reread ch1-context-p8 (cites it): Enigma's 158 quintillion settings, its never-itself flaw and the Bombe, but not how the machine works. Lost: what the machine is (keyboard, rotors, reflector, lamps) and one key lighting a different lamp at each press. Keep.

intent: Real thing: a glowing tube and a sliver of crystal each let a small signal switch a large current.
content: A glowing vacuum tube and a sliver of crystal each let a small control signal switch a large current because both are the same switch, so the transistor does the tube's job with no glass, filament or heat to burn out.
knows: A light switch; vacuum tubes as glass bulbs controlling current (ch1-transistor-p1).
subtraction: Reread ch1-transistor-p1 and p2: the vacuum tube as a glass bulb with a heated filament, ENIAC's 17,468 of them, and the transistor's invention; neither says how the two look. Lost: a tube and a transistor side by side as they look; 'the same job' is said only in the caption (ch1-transistor-p3). Half of one idea with Fig 1.4: the parts as they look, then the switch working. Placement: the merged card sits at Fig 1.4's slot, after ch1-transistor-p4 and p5, which teach the base its second half needs.
concepts_tried: Concepts for the merged card (drafted 2026-10-24 while the calibration page is up; stills only). B: one lamp circuit, the switch slot holding a tube on one side and a transistor on the other (its still shows only 'on'; the off state needs motion). C: the two at true relative scale on a 10 cm ruler (scale, but no function).
chosen: A, to build in Phase 2: a two-part card, the tube (1906) and the transistor (1947) drawn as they look on top; below, the transistor in Fig 1.5's lamp circuit, dark at 0 V on the base and lit at 0.7 V. Real thing, then function.

intent: Function: a small voltage on the base opens the path, so the lamp lights; without it, the lamp stays dark.
content: The lamp stays dark at 0 V on the base and lights at 0.7 V because the base voltage opens the path from collector to emitter, so one small voltage turns a current off or on: 0 or 1.

intent: Function: a positive gate pulls electrons under the oxide into a channel, so current flows only while it is on.
content: Electrons gather under the oxide into a channel when the gate goes positive because the gate's field pulls them up from the n-type source and drain (silicon with spare electrons) into the p-type body between, without touching them, so current flows only while the gate is on.
knows: A rubbed balloon lifting hair; a transistor as a switch (ch1-transistor-p4).
subtraction: Reread ch1-transistor-p7 and p18 (p18 cites it): doping, source, drain and gate, the barrier and the bridge of electrons, in dense words. Lost: the channel seen forming under the gate at 1 V and absent at 0 V. Keep.

intent: Function: transistor counts doubled about every two years, so on a tenfold-per-step scale they rise in a straight line.
content: The count of transistors per chip climbs a straight line on a log scale because it doubled about every two years, so 2,300 in 1971 becomes 28 billion in 2024, and the dots fall below the line after about 2015.
knows: Doubling (1, 2, 4, 8); a chart with years along the bottom.
subtraction: Reread ch1-transistor-p10: Moore's doubling, its revision to two years and its end around 2015, as a claim. Lost: the evidence, 2,300 transistors in 1971 to 28 billion in 2024 on a straight line on a log scale, then falling below it. Keep.

intent: Real thing: ENIAC's room of cabinets and a fingertip-sized chip do the same switching, 79 years apart.
content: ENIAC's thirty metres of cabinets and the M4 under a fingertip stand side by side, each at its own scale, because both do the same job of switching, so 17,468 tubes against 28 billion transistors shows 79 years of shrinking.
knows: A room full of cabinets; a fingertip; Fig 1.6's doubling.

intent: Function: the program sits in memory beside its data, so the CPU fetches each instruction like a number.
content: Instructions and numbers travel one at a time from one memory over one bus to the CPU because the program is stored as numbers beside its data, so as the program counter steps through cells 0, 1 and 2, load A, add B, store C turns 5 and 3 into 8 in cell C.
knows: Numbered boxes holding notes; Fig 1.1's head following stored rules.
subtraction: Reread ch1-vonneumann-p3 and p4 (p4 walks the figure cell by cell and cites it; ch1-cpu-p2 and ch2-arithmetic-p7 cite it too). Lost: one memory holding program and data, seen, as load A, add B and store C run over the bus. The prose depends on it. Keep.

intent: Function: the program counter advances by each instruction's length and the jump resets it, so the program loops.
content: The program counter moves 0x00, 0x05, 0x08 and back to 0x00 because each fetch advances it by the instruction's length and the jump resets it, so fetch, decode, execute and writeback repeat as a loop.
knows: Fig 1.8's memory cells; a recipe followed step by step.
subtraction: Reread ch1-cpu-p1 and p2 (p2 cites it): the four steps and instructions of different lengths, in words. Lost: the program counter seen stepping by each instruction's length (0x00, 0x05, 0x08) and jumping back. Keep.

intent: Function: the assembler turns mov eax, 5 into bytes: first the operation and register, then the value.
content: mov eax, 5 becomes five bytes, B8 05 00 00 00, because the assembler writes one byte for the operation and register and four for the value, lowest byte first, so the CPU reads B8 as "into EAX" and the rest as 5.
knows: Fig 1.9's instructions in memory; writing a number in digits.
subtraction: Reread ch1-cpu-p4 and p5: the ISA, assembly, and the bits of mov eax, 5 written out. Byte order leaves the book; no later passage or figure reads a value byte by byte, so nothing builds on it. A cut rewrites one citation, in Fig 1.9's How it works.

intent: Function: stages overlap like an assembly line, so once the line is full one instruction finishes every cycle.
content: Five instructions overlap stage by stage because each stage takes the next instruction as soon as it is free, so they finish in 9 cycles instead of 25, one instruction per cycle once the line is full.

content: One job ran at a time; between jobs the machine sat idle while the operator loaded the next card deck (about 25 idle minutes in an illustrative hour; your job runs ten). ch1-kernel-p3's idleness during a job, waiting for I/O, is a separate point.

intent: Function: a program cannot reach the disk itself; it must ask the kernel, which checks and does the work.
content: A program's direct reach for the disk is blocked while its system call goes through a fixed entry because the CPU runs programs in Ring 3 and the kernel in Ring 0, so the kernel checks every request and drives the device itself.
knows: A bank clerk fetches from the vault for you; Fig 1.13's shared machine.
subtraction: Reread ch1-kernel-p4 (cites it: time-sharing, the kernel, asking the kernel) and p6 after it (the system call, Ring 3 and Ring 0). Keep.

intent: Function: each level down is bigger but slower, so a cache keeps recent reads close and repeats are fast.
content: Each level from registers down to disk is bigger and slower (one second to six months, at a human scale) because faster memory costs more per byte, so a cache keeps what was just read and the second read takes 4 s instead of 3 min.
knows: A desk, a shelf and a library across town.
subtraction: Reread ch1-memory-p1 and p2: the hierarchy and three raw times (0.3 ns, 60 ns, 50,000 ns). Lost: the levels side by side at a human time scale, a register in a second, a disk in months. Keep.

intent: Function: binary splits a wire's voltage into two wide bands, so noise that tips ternary's narrow bands leaves binary right.
content: The same noise jostles two wires with the same span because binary splits it into two bands and ternary into three narrower ones, so binary reads all five bits right while ternary misreads its fourth digit.
knows: An on/off switch against a dimmer; a transistor switched by a voltage (ch1-transistor-p4).
subtraction: Reread ch2-binary-p2 and p3: one threshold against two, and narrow bands misread under drift, in words. Lost: the same noise on two wires, binary reading all five bits right and ternary misreading its fourth digit. Keep.

intent: Function: Boole's AND and two switches in series agree in every case, so algebra and circuit are one rule.
content: Boole's A · B and Shannon's two switches in series give the same answer in every case because each is true only when both inputs are, so the algebra of 1854 and the circuit of 1937 are one AND.
knows: And in everyday speech; two switches in a row (ch1-transistor-p5).
subtraction: Reread ch2-boole-p3 (AND true only when both are) and p6 (two relays in series as AND). Lost: the two halves side by side, Boole's overlap of two circles and two switches in series, as one rule. Already two-part. Keep.

intent: Function: as the inputs step through every case, each gate's output follows its rule: AND both, OR either, NOT the opposite.
content: Each gate's output follows its inputs as they step through every case because of the switches inside it (two in series for AND, two in parallel for OR, two taking turns for NOT), so each standard symbol's truth table fills row by row. Each standard symbol beside its truth table; the switches inside (two in series for AND, two in parallel for OR, two taking turns for NOT) are told in ch2-gates-p2.
knows: Fig 2.2's AND; switches in series and in parallel.
subtraction: Reread ch2-gates-p1 and p2: what a gate is, and the transistor wiring of AND, OR and NOT. Lost: the standard symbols and their truth tables as the inputs step through every case, which Figs 2.4 to 2.6 build on; neither paragraph draws a symbol or gives a table. Keep.

intent: Function: NAND is AND inverted, so tied inputs give NOT and inverting again gives AND: one gate builds all.
content: NOT, AND and OR are wired from NAND gates alone and give the same truth tables because NAND is AND inverted and two inversions cancel, so one kind of gate can build any circuit.
knows: Fig 2.3's three gates and their tables.
subtraction: Reread ch2-gates-p4 and p5: all three NAND constructions walked in words; no prose cites the figure (p4 points only at the De Morgan box). Lost: the three wirings seen at once as the inputs step through every case; p4 asks the reader to hold all three in mind. Keep.

intent: Function: each column needs the carry from its right, so carries ripple left and the answer settles bit by bit.
content: Adding 0101 and 0011, each full adder waits for the carry from its right-hand neighbour because a column's sum depends on it, so the carry ripples left and 1000 (8) settles one bit at a time.
knows: Carrying in column addition by hand; Fig 2.3's gates.
subtraction: Reread ch2-arithmetic-p5 to p7: the full adder and the ripple-carry chain, in words (cited by ch2-arithmetic-p9). Lost: the carry seen rippling left as 5 + 3 settles into 1000, one bit at a time. Keep.

intent: Function: two half adders and an OR turn the input bits into a sum bit and a carry.
content: Inside one full adder, two half adders (XOR for the sum, AND for the carry) and an OR produce sum and carry-out because XOR is 1 when the bits differ and AND when both are 1, so all eight input cases come out right.
knows: Fig 2.5's full adder as a box; Fig 2.3's gates.
subtraction: Reread ch2-arithmetic-p3 to p5: p5 gives the full adder in words (two half adders, the second adds the carry-in, the OR merges their carries, never both 1). Lost: the wiring seen, and the eight cases that let the reader check p5's claim that the two carries are never both 1. Keep.

intent: Function: adding a number's two's-complement pattern and dropping the carry out subtracts it, so the adder does both.
content: 7 plus 11111011 (the 8-bit pattern for −5: 5's bits flipped, plus 1) runs on the ordinary adder and a ninth bit falls off because 11111011 is 256 − 5 and the register holds eight bits, so exactly 2 remains: subtraction done by addition.
knows: Column addition (Fig 2.5); a car's odometer rolling over.
subtraction: Reread ch2-twos-p5 and p6: p6 works 7 − 5 in full (7 + 251 = 256 + 2, the ninth place dropped) and gives the hardware (NOT gates, a carry-in of 1). Lost: the bits seen in columns with the ninth bit falling off. Half of one idea with Fig 2.8: the subtraction in bits, then the wheel it runs on. Placement: the merged card sits at Fig 2.8's slot, after ch2-twos-p8, which gives the range the wheel draws.

intent: Function: a byte's values sit on a wheel, so adding past +127 wraps silently to −128.
content: A pointer turns one notch per +1 around a wheel of 256 values, the half whose top bit is 1 reading as negatives, because a byte wraps instead of growing, so +127 + 1 lands on −128 and −1 + 1 on 0, the same wrap that makes Fig 2.7's subtraction work.

content: 6.5 and −0.75 are read straight off their bits because a double stores a sign, an exponent that moves the point and a mantissa of digits, so 1.625 × 2² = 6.5 appears from the three fields.

content: On a line drawn to scale near 0.3, the true sum of the stored 0.1 and 0.2 falls exactly halfway between two doubles because both stored values sit slightly high, so the tie rounds up and prints 0.30000000000000004.

intent: Function: each tick of a tenth of a second ran slightly short, so the error grew until the radar missed.
content: The clock's error grows tick by tick to 0.34 s after 100 hours because 0.1 was stored cut short, a little under a ten-millionth of a second per tick, and each tick added the shortfall, so the radar looked about 570 m from the Scud and the battery never fired.

intent: Function: each instruction set encodes the same add in its own bits, so a program for one CPU fails elsewhere.
content: Add 5 to a register appears as 32 bits in three instruction sets because each packs the same opcode, register and 5 in its own order, so a program built for one CPU means nothing to another.

content: Three Intel lines become six ARM lines, registers and memory drawn apart so the extra lines are visibly trips to memory, because ARM cannot add in memory and must load, add and store, so Rosetta 2 translates the app once, before it runs.

content: One 64-bit register is shown nested as RAX, EAX, AX, then AH and AL because each generation (1978, 1985, 2003) widened it and kept the old names, so writing AL changes one byte and writing EAX clears the upper half.

subtraction: Reread ch3-registers-p1 and p2: 16 registers of 64 bits and six roles (RAX, RDI, RSI, RSP, RBP, RIP). Lost: the nesting seen, RAX holding EAX holding AX split into AH and AL, with dates; AX, AH and AL appear only in the card and its caption. Keep.

intent: Function: a shared convention fixes where each argument and the result go, so any compiler's code calls any other's.
content: add(5, 3) puts 5 in EDI and 3 in ESI, and 8 comes back in EAX, because every compiler follows the System V convention (first six arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9, the seventh on the stack), so code from any compiler can call any other.
knows: Fig 3.3's registers; handing things over in an agreed order.
subtraction: Reread ch3-registers-p2 and its summary table, which lists RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8 and R9 as the first six argument registers and RAX for the result. A cut rewrites ch3-call-p2's citation and Fig BR.2's How it works; a third citation, ch3-defenses-p8, sits in held material: listed for the owner.

intent: Function: every process's stack grows down from under the kernel, so each call grows it and each return shrinks it.
content: A process's memory runs from code and data at the bottom, the heap growing up and the stack growing down from under the kernel because the operating system gives every process the same layout, so each call adds a frame and each return removes it.
knows: Fig 1.8's numbered memory; a stack of plates.
subtraction: Reread ch3-stack-p1: the address space, and the stack placed high and growing down (cited by ch3-stack-p4). Keep.

content: The stack and RIP change step by step through one call of add because call saves where to come back to and ret jumps there, so the program carries on exactly after the call with the result in RAX.

intent: Function: the CPU checks a privilege bit, so in Ring 3 a privileged instruction never runs; the kernel takes over.
content: The same three instructions run in Ring 3 and in Ring 0 because the CPU checks a privilege bit on each, so add runs in both while the two privileged ones stop at #GP in Ring 3 and jump to the kernel's handler.

subtraction: Reread chBridge-mode-p3 and p4: the CPU checking the CPL, #GP, and the Ring 0 instructions, in words. Lost: the same three instructions in each ring side by side, add running in both and the two privileged ones stopping at #GP in Ring 3. Keep.

intent: Function: SYSCALL jumps to an address the kernel chose, so a program picks the service, never the destination.
content: One write call crosses from Ring 3 to Ring 0 and back because SYSCALL saves where to return and jumps to an address the kernel registered, with the request number in RAX, so the program picks the service but never the destination, and SYSRET brings it back in under a microsecond.
knows: Fig BR.1's privilege bit; Fig 1.14's system call.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-trap-p1 and p2 (p2 cites it, as does chBridge-trap-p4): the trap, the number in RAX, SYSCALL, the saved address and SYSRET, in words. Lost: the round trip in time order, with the registers that carry it. Keep.

intent: Function: a vector number picks an entry in the kernel's table, and the CPU jumps to that entry's handler.
content: A vector number picks one of 256 entries and the CPU jumps to that entry's handler because the kernel filled the table at boot and IDTR points to it, so exceptions (0–31), device interrupts (32 and up) and int 0x80 all enter the kernel the same way.
knows: Fig BR.2's trap; a building directory pointing to rooms.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-trap-p4 (cites it): exceptions, interrupts, vectors and the IDT, in words. Lost: the table itself, its vectors and their sources, and the lookup through IDTR. Corrected on owner-calls (§4af). Keep.

intent: Function: the MMU translates every address and checks its permissions, so a forbidden access never reaches memory.
content: A virtual address passes through the MMU before it reaches RAM because the MMU translates the page number through the page tables and checks the permission bits, so a forbidden access never reaches memory and becomes a page fault.
knows: Fig 3.5's per-process address space; Fig 1.15's caches.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-mode-p7 and chBridge-mmu-p1 and p2: the MMU between CPU and RAM, translation and the permission check, in words. Lost: one store stopped by the permission check, and the order of the steps (translate, check, fault), seen. Its TLB step belongs to Fig BR.5; the two carry separate ideas, so no merge.

intent: Function: programs reuse the same few pages, so the TLB answers most translations and the slow walk runs rarely.
content: Most accesses are answered at once by the TLB because programs touch the same few pages again and again, so only a miss pays the four-read walk, and its translation replaces the entry used longest ago.
knows: A page-table walk (chBridge-mmu-p2); Fig 1.15's cache keeping the last read.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-mmu-p5: the four-read walk and the TLB with its hit rate, in words. Lost: locality seen keeping the walk rare, and the entry used longest ago replaced on a miss.

intent: Function: the hardware timer interrupts whatever runs, so the kernel gets the CPU back even from an endless loop.
content: Every millisecond a timer tick hands the core to the kernel's scheduler, which saves the running process's registers and loads the next one's, because the hardware timer interrupts whatever is running, so even C, stuck in an endless loop, loses the CPU like the others.
knows: A kitchen timer; Fig BR.3's interrupts.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-timer-p1 and p2: without a timer one stuck program freezes the machine; the tick and the kernel's work at it, in words. Lost: preemption seen over four milliseconds, the stuck process C losing the CPU like the others. Keep.

intent: Function: devices sit at addresses among the RAM, so an ordinary store can change the screen or set a timer.
content: One flat physical address range holds RAM, the GPU's frame buffer and each core's interrupt controller because device registers sit at fixed addresses, so the same store saves a value, changes a pixel or sets the timer by address alone.
knows: Fig 1.8's numbered memory cells.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-io-p1 and p2: MMIO and DMA named and defined. Lost: the physical address map seen, device ranges (frame buffer, local APIC) among the RAM, the same store doing different work by address. Keep.

intent: Function: the device copies data into RAM by itself, so the CPU runs other work until an interrupt says done.
content: The kernel queues a command and rings the doorbell, the drive fills the buffer itself while B runs, and an interrupt wakes A because the device can write RAM without the CPU, so the CPU keeps working during the read.
knows: Fig BR.7's device registers; Fig BR.6's interrupts.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-io-p4: the NVMe read in long words (queue, doorbell, DMA, interrupt). Lost: the three steps seen with process B running meanwhile. Keep.

intent: Function: each abstraction rests on one hardware feature the kernel sets up, so removing that feature removes the abstraction.
content: Five hardware features on the left become, through the kernel, the abstractions on the right because each service rests on one feature, so take the MMU away and separate processes go with it, take the timer away and nothing can stop a program that never yields.
knows: The five features drawn in Figs BR.1 to BR.8.
